cards.back: Globular protein catalyst (a few are RNA) that speeds a reaction by lowering activation energy — never consumed by it.
Region of the enzyme whose shape and charge properties are complementary to one specific substrate; reaction happens here.
Substrate binding induces a shape change in the active site, improving catalysis (replaces the rigid lock-and-key idea).
Minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur. Enzymes lower Eᴀ — they do not change ΔG or the equilibrium.
Permanent loss of tertiary structure (weak bonds broken) → distorted active site → no function. Caused by heat above optimum or pH outside range.
Inhibitor resembles the substrate and occupies the active site. Raising substrate concentration outcompetes it.
Inhibitor binds an allosteric site, distorting the active site. Raising substrate concentration does NOT restore rate.
Binding site away from the active site — target of non-competitive inhibitors and end-product regulators.
Final product of a pathway allosterically inhibits the first enzyme — negative feedback (e.g. isoleucine inhibiting the threonine pathway).
Anabolism builds (usually condensation, energy-requiring); catabolism breaks down (usually hydrolysis, energy-releasing).
Cofactor: inorganic ion helper (Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺). Coenzyme: organic helper, often vitamin-derived.

cards.front: Why does reaction rate plateau at high substrate concentration?
cards.back: All active sites are occupied — the enzyme becomes the limiting factor. Rate then depends on enzyme concentration.

cards.front: Describe the rate–temperature curve for an enzyme.
cards.back: Rises below the optimum (more kinetic energy, more successful collisions); falls steeply above it (heat breaks hydrogen bonds → denaturation). Asymmetric shape.

cards.front: Why does pH affect enzyme activity?
cards.back: pH changes charges on amino acid side chains in the active site → substrate binds less well → extremes denature the enzyme. Optimum matches the enzyme's environment (stomach ≈ 2, intestine ≈ 7).

cards.front: Catalase/H₂O₂ filter-paper experiment — how is rate measured?
cards.back: Time for disks to rise to the surface: O₂ bubbles lift them. Faster rise = faster rate. Vary one factor (e.g. [H₂O₂] or temperature), control the rest.

cards.front: Why include a boiled-enzyme tube in the catalase experiment?
cards.back: Negative control: shows no O₂ production without active enzyme — proves observed change is enzyme-dependent (an IA design criterion).

cards.front: Two advantages of immobilised enzymes in industry?
cards.back: Reusable and easily separated from the product; often more heat-stable (e.g. lactose-free milk).
Explain = give reasons/causes with a mechanism. State = short answer, no reasoning. Matching the verb to the answer shape earns the marks.

cards.front: Which enzymes are the exception to “all enzymes are proteins”?
cards.back: Ribozymes — catalytic RNA molecules. Almost everything else is a globular protein.
